questions.question: A science teacher lists four changes for her class to sort, and she warns them that a showy change is not always a chemical one. Which of the four makes a new substance?
questions.answer: A firework bursting in the night sky
choices: A firework bursting in the night sky
Dry ice giving off a cold white fog
Sweat drying on a runner's skin
A geode split open with a hammer
questions.context: A firework's black powder burns in a flash and turns into new substances, mostly nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour, whose rushing gases burst the shell. Dry ice only turns straight into carbon dioxide gas, and its fog is water from the air condensed by the cold. Drying sweat is water evaporating, and the split geode holds the same crystals as before.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade asks students to classify new cases as physical or chemical changes, and a firework is a standard example of a chemical one.

questions.question: A glass beaker slips from a student's hand and shatters on the lab floor, and its pieces can never be fitted back into a beaker. Her lab partner says that a change that cannot be undone must be a chemical change. Why is he wrong?
questions.answer: Each broken piece is still glass
choices: Each broken piece is still glass
Glass is far too hard a material to react
The break happened far too fast for a reaction
Only liquids and gases can take part in reactions
questions.context: A chemical change makes a new substance, and every shard is the same glass as before, so shattering is a physical change, however hard it is to undo; melted down, the pieces make glass again. Hardness and speed decide nothing: hydrofluoric acid etches hard glass, a firework reacts in a flash, and solid iron rusts.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that a new substance, not whether a change can be undone, makes a change chemical, and breaking glass is its classic physical change.

questions.question: A silver cup stands for years in a museum case and slowly grows a thin black film of tarnish. The film is a new substance, made when the silver joins with an element carried by a gas in the air. Which element joins the silver?
choices: Sulfur
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Carbon
questions.context: Traces of sulfur gases in the air, mostly hydrogen sulfide given off by things such as wool and rubber, react with silver and make black silver sulfide. Rust is iron joined with oxygen, but silver tarnish holds no oxygen at all. Each polishing rubs away a little of the silver along with the film.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade lists the tarnishing of silver among its standard chemical changes, and guessing an oxide like rust is the usual mix-up.

questions.question: Michael Faraday lectured to young people at the Royal Institution in London on the chemistry of a candle. He blew a candle out and held a flame in the vapour rising from its wick, and fire ran down through the air and lit the candle again. What was the vapour?
choices: Wax turned into a gas
Steam made by the burning wax
Carbon dioxide from the flame
Air heated by the flame
questions.context: The flame melts the wax, the liquid climbs the wick, and the heat turns it into a gas: changes of state that leave it wax, still able to burn. Only the burning in the flame is a chemical change, and it makes carbon dioxide and water vapour, which cannot burn. Air is no fuel either, so only the wax vapour could carry the fire back to the wick.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade sorts a burning candle's changes into physical and chemical ones, and Faraday's candle lectures are the classic story of them.

questions.question: A student strikes a match and lets it burn down to a thin black stick, while smoke and hot gases rise from the flame. No physical means, such as heating, cooling, pressing or soaking, can turn the black stick back into fresh wood. Why not?
questions.answer: The wood has become new substances
choices: The wood has become new substances
The wood has melted out of its shape
The wood's heat has escaped into the air
The wood is coated in soot that will not wash off
questions.context: Burning joins the wood's substances with oxygen and turns them into carbon dioxide, water vapour and ash, and the black stick left is charcoal, mostly carbon. No change of shape, size or state can turn new substances back into wood. Wood does not melt in a flame, and the black stick is charcoal itself, not wood under a coat of soot.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade gives burning a match as a chemical change and explains it by the new substances that burning makes.

questions.question: A student stirs a scoop of salt into a beaker of water until no grains can be seen. Her teacher asks for proof that no new substance was made and that the dissolving was only a physical change. Which observation gives that proof?
questions.answer: Drying the water away leaves salt again
choices: Drying the water away leaves salt again
No grains of salt can be seen any more
The salt water weighs as much as both did
The water stays clear and colourless
questions.context: When the water is dried away the same salt is left, so it was there all along, spread through the water in bits too small to see; salt works make salt from seawater this way. A solid also vanishes into a clear liquid in some chemical changes, as zinc does in acid, and mass is kept in every change. So vanishing, a clear liquid and the same mass prove nothing; getting the salt back does.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade explains why dissolving salt is a physical change: the salt can be got back by evaporating the water.

questions.question: A teacher touches the ends of a 9-volt battery to a pad of fine steel wool, which is mostly iron. The wool glows and burns with sparks, leaving a dark, brittle mass. How is this burning like the slow rusting of an iron nail left out in the rain?
choices: Both join iron with oxygen
Both need water to happen
Both give off a bright light
Both need heat to get started
questions.context: In both, iron joins with oxygen from the air and becomes iron oxide, a new substance, so both are chemical changes. The thin wool reacts in seconds and needs no water, while the nail takes months and rusts only where it is wet. Rusting gives off no light and needs no spark or flame to start it.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names rusting and burning as chemical changes and teaches rusting as iron slowly joining with oxygen.

questions.question: Rainwater, made a weak acid by carbon dioxide from the air, slowly works on the hard feldspar crystals in a granite boulder. Over many years they turn into a soft, white clay that can be moulded when wet. What is the clay?
questions.answer: A new mineral made from the feldspar
choices: A new mineral made from the feldspar
Feldspar ground into a very fine powder
Quartz grains worn loose from the granite
Mud washed in by the rain from elsewhere
questions.context: The acid in the rain reacts with the feldspar and turns it into kaolinite, a clay mineral with new properties, so this is chemical weathering. Ice splitting rock in its cracks is physical weathering, since the pieces are the same minerals, only smaller. Quartz, another of granite's minerals, resists this weathering.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade earth science sorts weathering into physical and chemical, and feldspar turning into clay is the standard example of the chemical kind.

questions.question: A bite of food goes through several changes in the mouth before it is swallowed. Most of them change only its size or shape, as crushing changes a rock, but one makes a new substance. Which change is that?
choices: Saliva breaking starch into sugar
Teeth grinding food into crumbs
Saliva wetting food into a soft lump
The tongue rolling food into a ball
questions.context: Amylase, an enzyme in saliva, breaks starch into simpler sugars, new substances, so this is chemical digestion. Grinding, wetting and rolling change only the food's size and shape: mechanical digestion, a physical change. The stomach's churning is mechanical digestion too.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade body systems teach mechanical and chemical digestion, a physical and a chemical change at work in the mouth.

questions.question: Inside an old-style light bulb, a thin wire of the metal tungsten glows white-hot whenever the bulb is switched on, giving off light and a great deal of heat. Is the glowing wire going through a chemical change?
questions.answer: No, the wire stays tungsten all along
choices: No, the wire stays tungsten all along
Yes, it gives off light and heat
Yes, the wire is slowly burning up
No, metals cannot take part in reactions
questions.context: Light and heat are only clues: the current heats the wire until it glows, and it is still tungsten when it cools, so the glow is a physical change. The bulb holds a vacuum or an unreactive gas, with no oxygen for the wire to burn in, though metals do react, as rusting iron shows. The wire slowly thins as tungsten atoms escape from it as a gas, a change of state that makes no new substance.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade classifies new cases by asking whether a new substance forms, even when a change gives off light and heat.
